III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01687

Thus the outline of every material object has six faces, six directions: below and above, behind and in front, left and right. The six faces of a physical solid are the hexaemeron, the six ever-present “days” of Creation. (Exactly the same argument appears in Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î: the geometrical boundaries of a solid are the six simultaneous “days” of its creation.) And the seventh day? The seventh day is the whole itself—the solid or physical person that supports and completes those six faces. It is also the whole's dimension beyond the senses, for it is the soul that perceives form as a whole. As the “seventh” face of a solid with six sides and three dimensions, the “seventh day” is, in a sense, its “fourth” dimension.
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01688
Considered in relation to the cosmos as a whole, it is the Human Form that completes the cosmic process and carries it beyond itself.
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01689

Considered in relation to the sacred cosmos, the spiritual world, it is the Form of the Resurrector, the last Imam. By announcing the Resurrection of Resurrections (qiyâmat al-qiyâmât), he will inaugurate our world's passage from its present cycle of concealment (dawr al-satr) into the cycle of manifestation (dawr al-kashf) destined to follow it.
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01690

We have now reached a higher level of Ismaili spiritual interpretation, “the esoteric within the esoteric.” Here the six days of the creation of the sacred cosmos are the six great prophets entrusted with a Revelation, the six periods of the complete cycle of prophecy. A prophet's “day” is the period belonging to that prophet, from the moment he is called until the coming of the Imam who closes his period. There have been the “days” of Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Christ, and Mohammad.
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01691

“If people understood this spiritual interpretation,” Nâsir-e Khosraw writes, “they would see the prophetic religions standing in their proper places, where each was brought forth: the Mazdeans on the third day, the Jews on the fourth day, the Christians on the fifth day, Islam on the sixth day.” The Qur'anic verse speaks of the creation of the Heavens (plural) and the Earth (singular) to signify that the outward forms of religions are many and appear to be in conflict, while their inward meaning—their ta'wîl—is one.
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01692

The Throne upon which the Merciful establishes himself on the seventh day is the person of the Resurrector (Qâ'im), the last Imam, through whom and in whom the inward meaning of all Revelations will be unveiled. The last Imam himself is the “seventh day.” His person gathers together and sums up the “six days” of prophecy, just as the complete form of a physical solid gathers together its six faces. At different levels of meaning, both complete and recapitulate the “six days of Creation.”
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01693

The whole secret history of humankind—the six millennia symbolizing the cycle of prophecy—moves toward the appearance of this perfect Human Form, the Resurrecting Imam (al-walad al-tâmm, the Perfect Child). His millennium, the seventh in the cycle, is the seventh day of the creation of the sacred cosmos. For no one, not even one of the six great prophets, has yet received the fullness of everything. The seventh day has not yet dawned: “the day when no soul shall have power over another soul, and the command shall belong to God alone” (82:19).
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01694

There is, of course, a difference between the eschatology of Twelver Shiism and Shaykhism on the one hand and that of Ismaili Shiism on the other. I think we can express it most briefly by saying that Twelver teachings about the Imam correspond symbolically to the heaven of the fixed stars, the sphere of the twelve constellations of the zodiac, whereas Ismaili teachings correspond to the seven planetary heavens and their moving stars.
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01695

For Twelver Shiites, the last Imam is already here. He has already appeared, but his divine splendor is now hidden in a world beyond the senses until the hour of his manifestation or parousia. For the Ismailis, the last Imam is the secret of the future, the Form of superhuman perfection that humanity will bring forth on the Last Day. That day cannot dawn until the whole cycle of planetary revolutions is complete.
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01696

Yet on both sides the “time of the Imam” takes spatial form as an Earth beyond this Earth: among the Shaykhis, the mystical Earth of Hûrqalyâ; among the Ismailis, the Earth mentioned in the Qur'anic verse concerning the creation of the Heavens and the Earth. This cannot mean our present Earth, for Scripture says it is “illumined by the light of its Lord.”
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01697

Our Earth, by contrast, remains in Darkness, although the light of physical day shines upon it. No: the verse concerns the mystical hexaemeron, “that other Earth, still concealed in the night ... upon which, it is said, the esoteric community is already established through the steadfastness of faith, not through any material settlement ... and which is the Earth of light.” On that Earth the darkness of religions confined to the literal word and the Law will have been dispersed.
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01698

This, in the broadest outline, is how the texts of Shaykhi Twelver Gnosis and Ismaili Gnosis present the structural correspondence of time and space. I believe we could easily verify here the laws of “hermeneutic perspective,” the perspective opened by spiritual interpretation, which we sketched in Book I of the present work. At the same time, an intellectual undertaking comes into view.
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01699

Though it works specifically upon the forms of biblical or Qur'anic Revelation, it differs neither in scope nor in intention—only in method—from contemporary efforts to analyze and bring together the harmonic forms perceived throughout Nature, in every kingdom and at every level of the universe. It is as true to say that living beings grow and live in time but die and disappear in space as it is to say that they grow in space and likewise vanish in time.
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01700

The opposition between time and space, their separation and their power to destroy one another, is experienced as something demonic. That is the tragedy of every living creature: having to fulfill its task in time, only to surrender everything it acquired or won in space during that time—and the reverse is equally true.
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01701

Thus the symmorphosis of form in time and form in space, abolishing the law by which each destroys the other, is envisioned in Shiite spiritual philosophy as the “form of Resurrection,” the “perfect form of the Imam,” the “Earth of Light,” and the “seventh day of Creation.”
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01702

Seen in this light, Shiite eschatology offers its own resolution of the tragedy faced by every living being: thrown into time, yet feeling within itself an insistent presence that protests against its destruction by time. The Imam's space—the “Earth of Light of Hûrqalyâ,” where time becomes space—appears as salvation from chronological time.
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01703

This brings the Imam's person fully into view at the “supreme horizon” to which Shiite thought and spirituality raise him. It seems to us, then, that this work can end in no other way than by turning to the person of the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam. Century after century, his presence endures in Shiite consciousness, entering the lives of believers, the mighty and the humble alike, in moments of doubt, distress, and abandonment. Whether in dreams or in waking life, a fleeting vision shines with trust in the Unseen and the certainty that his presence is always near.

Chapter I The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
en-book-7-ch-1-s1
1. The Completion of the Fullness of the Twelve
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01705

We have spoken of the Twelfth Imam so often that any attempt to collect all those passages here would risk repetition. Readers wishing to keep in mind everything implied by the completion of the fullness—the pleroma—of the Twelve should refer to our earlier discussions of the doctrine of the Imams. With that groundwork established, we must now outline the portrait offered by the hagiography, or sacred biography, of the Twelfth Imam. This biography is still unfinished, for it continues throughout his “occultation” (ghaybat), the period of his hidden presence.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01706
We shall then explore certain parallels between the ideas surrounding him and themes familiar in the West, grouping them chiefly under spiritual chivalry and the reign of the Paraclete.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01707

Let us begin by recalling, first, some sayings of the Prophet concerning the Twelve Imams, and especially the Twelfth; and second, the law of sacred rhythm that determines their number. Both lead to consequences that meet in the person of the Twelfth Imam, as Shiite consciousness understands him.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01708
Shiite writings about the Twelfth Imam are vast.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01709

First come the traditions recorded in various collections of hadîth. They concern both his brief manifestation in the past and his future manifestation—his parousia at the end of our Aeon—as the Imam who announces the Resurrection (Qâ'im al-qiyâmat), the one from Mohammad's family “who rises” for the Resurrection (Qâ'im âl Mohammad).
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01710

Between these two manifestations, the “history” of the Twelfth Imam continues. It consists of a great body of narratives and testimonies from people to whom he has appeared, whether in dreams or while awake, always in circumstances that go beyond the ordinary laws of sense perception and the accepted standards of rational evidence.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01711

As presented to Shiite consciousness in its collections of hadîth, neither the number of twelve Imams nor the completion of their fullness by the twelfth is an accident of history. In several traditions the Prophet solemnly announces that the Imams after him will number twelve, and no more. The last will be the Resurrector (Qâ'im), the Mahdi: the one who is guided and who guides others toward God.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01712

Another interpretation, based on the expression al-Mahdî ilay-hi, understands him as the one toward whom people are guided and who then becomes their guide (al-Mahdî al-Hâdî). Usually the Prophet announces the coming of the Mahdi, the Resurrector, in relation to his own prophetic mission as the bearer of the revealed letter (tanzîl). The Mahdi will be master of ta'wîl, spiritual interpretation: he will disclose the complete inward meaning of all divine Revelations. This idea is shared by Twelver Shiite and Ismaili Gnosis.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01713

In one hadîth, the Prophet calls the First Imam his brother and speaks of the Twelfth as though he were his own child. Someone asks him: “O Messenger of God, who is your child?” He replies: “The Mahdi, the one whom I was sent to announce.” Two other traditions deserve special mention.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01714

In one, the Prophet declares: “If only a single day remained to this world, God would lengthen that day so that a man of my descendants might arise in it, whose name will be my name and whose byname will be my byname. He will fill the Earth with peace and justice, just as it is now filled with violence and tyranny.”
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01715

In the second, after announcing that exactly nine Imams will follow Hosayn ibn 'Alî, the Third Imam, the Prophet adds: “The ninth will be the Qâ'im. He will fill the Earth with peace and justice, just as it is now filled with violence and tyranny. He will fight to restore the spiritual meaning (ta'wîl), just as I myself fought to reveal the literal meaning.”
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01716

These texts—and many more could be cited—show how firmly Shiite tradition believes that the Prophet's own teaching contains the essence of its understanding of prophecy and the Imams. At its heart lies a balance of complementary realities: outward and inward meaning, nobowwat and walâyat; the prophets' mission of disclosing the outward Revelation and the Imams' spiritual gift of initiating believers into its inward meaning. The Imamate of Mohammad's line, taken as a whole, is the Seal of universal walâyat, the spiritual guardianship and authority of the Imams. The Twelfth Imam in particular is the Seal of Muhammadan walâyat, in whom all walâyat is gathered together.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01717
Thus Shiite tradition believes it receives from the Prophet himself its deepest understanding of the Mahdi as the Seal of Muhammadan walâyat.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01718

This differs fundamentally from the conception of the Mahdi widespread in Sunni Islam. There, the Mahdi cannot be organically linked to the Imam in the specifically Shiite sense, and therefore cannot be linked in the same way to the inward meaning (bâtin) of Revelation or its spiritual interpretation (ta'wîl). Nor can the idea carry the same sense of a future still open to human expectation after the coming of the Seal of the Prophets.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01719

Here, by contrast, the last Prophet himself becomes the forerunner of the last Imam: the one who will interpret the Revelation the Prophet brought, and therefore the Imam of the Resurrection. As we have already emphasized, the fundamental difference lies in this way of envisaging the future. Shiism certainly agrees that Revelation is complete, that the cycle of divine communications has been closed and sealed, and that Mohammad was the Seal of the Prophets.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01720

But Shiite tradition sees the closing of the prophetic mission as the signal for the opening of a new cycle: the cycle of walâyat, of spiritual initiation. Shiite consciousness has heard with particular anguish the declaration that humanity, in its distress, has no further prophet to await.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01721
Yet the last Prophet himself announced the one who was still to be awaited: the Imam, Seal of Muhammadan walâyat, is the Awaited Imam (montazar).
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01722

Hence that restless serenity, that hidden movement, that union of radical pessimism with unconquerable hope which we have already recognized in Shiite consciousness and described as desperatio fiducialis: a despair that nevertheless trusts.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01723

There is another consideration. Alongside these texts establishing the necessary bond between the Seal of the Prophets and the Twelfth Imam—the Seal of Muhammadan walâyat—and affirming the identity of their names and the symmetry of their missions, there are numerous hadîth insisting on the sacred rhythm that fixes the number of Imams at twelve. These traditions prevent us from explaining the end of the visible manifestation of the Imams' fullness on Earth as some historical accident comparable to the events that brought worldly dynasties to an end.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01724

Their number is connected with the significance of twelve: the twelve signs of the zodiac, the twelve months of the year, the twelve hours of day and of night, the twelve leaders of the tribes of Israel, and so on. Likewise, within the scheme of Shiite sacred history, each of the six (or seven) great prophets was followed by twelve Imams.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01725

We should also recall the hadîth of the “Twelve Veils of Light.” Represented as twelve millennia, these Veils express within Shiism the ancient theologies of the Aeon. Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî gave a remarkable commentary on this tradition. In discussing it, we even spoke of a structural doctrine of the Imams: the twelvefold structure of the Imamate corresponds to the cubic temple of the Ka'ba, understood anew as a spiritual temple.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01726

But if the Prophet's own teaching about the Twelfth Imam implies that humanity's religious and spiritual history remains open—that sacred history, of which the facts of ordinary history are merely the chrysalis, is not yet complete—how can this be reconciled with the assertion that the Imamate is limited to twelve Imams and that the twelfth has already been born? Does that not mean that the Imamate itself is closed? Certainly not. Rather, it points to the profound idea at the heart of the Twelfth Imam's figure: the necessity of his concealment from this world, his ghaybat.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01727

The Imamate of the Twelve spans the entire interval between the close of prophecy and the Last Day. Since eleven Imams have already appeared, the twelfth must exist and endure in a manner not subject to the ordinary laws of biology or chronological time. Consequently, to everyone who remains in this world under those laws, his presence must take the paradoxical form of an absence. None of his mysterious appearances to the faithful brings his ghaybat to an end.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01728
But every such appearance suspends, for the believer who encounters him, the ordinary condition of human beings who cannot perceive the Imam's “hidden presence.”
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01729

This is why the time of the Hidden Imam is an interval, a time “between times.” His “history,” as it unfolds in the consciousness of his followers, is the ripening of that interval until another kind of time comes into being and brings the time of absence to an end. And this is why a believer who is granted a vision of him also finds himself “between times.” Such a vision is not an event within the time of this world, something that could be fitted into its history.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01730

The Imam's hidden presence is a not yet whose fulfillment remains perpetually close: it is the “imminent Hour” spoken of in sura 54. The coming of the awaited Imam is expressed by a single word, “Joy” (farah). No Shiite speaks or writes the name of the Twelfth Imam without adding the customary prayer: “May God hasten the Joy for us.”
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01731

The complete history of the Twelfth Imam therefore embraces the events of his manifestation in both past and future. Here “past” and “future” belong to the objective time of chronology, while the present of his hidden presence belongs to lived, existential time, a time “between” the times of chronology. Each event in his history breaks through History, for it cannot be contained within what we ordinarily call history, governed by what we call historical causation. Examples abound.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01732

To speak of Israel crossing the Red Sea is one thing; to speak of that same crossing as Israel's liberation from bondage to matter and entry into the supernatural spiritual world is another. Above all, we must follow the path shown us by our philosopher-theosophers, especially Qazi Sa'id Qommi, when they explain the time and place of the malakut, the spiritual world. The “history” of the Twelfth Imam is a sacred biography, and we shall try to set out its principal events.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01733

But a warning is needed at the outset. Once we cross the threshold into this sacred biography, what is usually called historical criticism will seem to have lost almost all its authority. If, however, we leave its demands at the threshold, and approach what is before us through a genuinely phenomenological perception—attending to the reality as it presents itself—we may become capable, through the appropriate faculty, of perceiving and understanding what events “between times” mean. We may also recognize the higher order of reality they announce, precisely because they belong to it.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01734
Every sacred biography can call upon witnesses, often many of them, as in the case of the Twelfth Imam.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01735

Yet it cannot produce the certificates, attestations, and documents demanded by our fixation on outward, material historicity. That fixation has left us able to imagine only one acceptable level of reality on which an “event” can occur. To demand that sacred biography supply documents of the kind used in critical history is already to lower the level of reality to which its events belong. That reduction has undoubtedly been going on for a long time.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01736

The less capable we are of perceiving that “events take place in Heaven,” the more insistently we demand proof of their material historicity. The more we lose our sense of events whose reality is essentially a mysterium liturgicum, a sacred mystery enacted in worship, the more festivals we erase from the calendar.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01737

What is today called “historical materialism” has distant predecessors, even within theology. Everything we shall report about the sacred biography of the Twelfth Imam may therefore seem, to a historian, to rest upon documents without objective value. And yet the events did happen!
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01738

But documents preserving the only traces that events occurring in the malakut can leave are merely discarded husks, empty chrysalises, if we lack the key to them. For any philosopher who accepts even a minimum of “spiritual realism,” on the other hand, these documents are beyond price.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01739

In other words, the faculty of perception required here is “that eye of the soul which never sleeps,” as Philo of Alexandria puts it. Events belonging to the time of the Twelfth Imam, whether recorded in documents concerned with past, present, or future, can be grasped only by the “spiritual senses” of which all our philosopher-theosophers speak. The Imam is absent from sensory perception; indeed, even if he stood physically before us, he would remain invisible as Imam to anyone who could see only as one sees ordinary objects in the external world. His epiphany, his coming into presence, cannot take place until human consciousness has awakened to it.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01740

In the interval “between times,” it can occur only for the few whom he himself chooses: those capable of spiritual recognition (ma'rifat), rather than the merely outward awareness of which even an animal is capable. This is what the texts taught us when they spoke of “seeing the Imam in Hurqalya.” They implied that the suprasensory world of Hurqalya and the material world of the senses coexist, penetrate one another, and contain one another.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01741

Hurqalya is above us, around us, and within us at the same time. If, through our ignorance, it is not within us, we can neither know nor recognize it “anywhere”; for we can know something outside ourselves only through a corresponding capacity within. To understand the Hidden Imam's concealed presence in this world, we might, outwardly speaking, compare him to the bodhisattva of Mahayana Buddhism, who renounces departure from this world and delays entry into nirvana until all those entrusted to him have been saved.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01742

Inwardly speaking, we might recall Mulla Sadra's teaching that every soul, every spiritual being, carries its own heaven or hell within itself. These are only indications of a way of understanding, a modus intelligendi, with a rigor of its own. Without such a way of understanding, we might as well confess ourselves unable to comprehend sacred knowledge, the perception of invisible worlds, and the visionary events of which sacred history is made.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01743

But for the seeker who “saves the phenomena” by approaching them as a pilgrim of sincere heart, these events will reveal, more fully than any theoretical account, the secret of the Shiite soul—a secret whose strength has withstood the powers of doubt and denial for ten centuries.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
en-book-7-ch-1-s2
2. From Byzantium to Samarra
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01744

The traditional account that opens the sacred biography of the Twelfth Imam begins with a young Christian princess of Byzantium. An Isolde-like love awakens in her heart, but hers is a love that calls her to give miraculous birth to a Divine Child. The theme of the Divine Child is well known in the history of religions; the Shiite texts concerning it, however, have received very little study. Here we shall present the essential story.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01745

The Tenth Imam, Ali Naqi, became Imam at the age of seven and died in 254/868, scarcely into his forties. He suffered particularly from the suspicions and harassment of the Abbasid caliph, who had turned Samarra, about a hundred kilometers north of Baghdad, into a military city. The caliph kept the Imam there, more or less a prisoner, for twenty years. It was there that the Imam's son Hasan was born in 231/845, and it was for this reason that he was called Hasan Askari, from askar, meaning “army.” There too, on the fifteenth of Sha'ban in the year 255 (3 August 868), was born Hasan's son, the Twelfth and last Imam.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01746

Granted divine foreknowledge, Imam Ali Naqi arranged matters so that his son could marry the woman destined to become the mother of the Twelfth Imam. Here sacred history begins. It unfolds through a supernatural correspondence between the Imam's foreknowledge and what can only be called the young Christian girl's initiation: a series of visionary dreams through which the future mother of the coming Imam must pass.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01747

What we have already explained about the cycle of prophecy and the successive reappearances of the fullness of the Twelve enables us to understand the possibilities of a spiritual fellowship between religions at the esoteric level. At the same time, the way these events are presented reveals how Shiism understands its relationship with Christianity; and there is something deeply moving in it.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01748

The accounts of the Twelfth Imam's birth and brief appearance on earth were gathered and organized by the first generation of great Shiite theologians. They trace back to contemporary witnesses who took part in the events.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01749

We shall chiefly follow the version given by the great theologian Ibn Babuyeh of Qom, known as Shaykh Saduq. His account claims to reproduce, word for word, the testimony of Bashar ibn Solayman Nahhas, a close associate and intimate companion of the two Imams, Ali Naqi and Hasan Askari, during their enforced residence at Samarra.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01750

One day, then, Imam Ali Naqi sent his servant Kafur to fetch Bashar. Once Bashar had taken his place before him, the Imam addressed him solemnly: “Bashar, you are our friend. You and your family have always shown the same devotion to the members of the Prophet's household. I wish to honor you with a privilege that will give you a place of friendship unequaled among our Shiites. I am going to entrust you with a secret and send you on a mission to bring a certain young woman here.”
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01751

The Imam then wrote a letter in Greek with his own hand, sealed it, and placed it in a red leather purse together with two hundred and twenty dinars. He gave Bashar the following instructions. Bashar was to go to Baghdad and, at the appointed hour, stand by the river at the harbor where ships carrying captive women came ashore. The only prospective buyers on the quay would be agents of the Abbasid caliph. Bashar was to spend the whole day watching, from a distance, what took place aboard a ship belonging to a man named Amr ibn Yazid.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01752

At a certain moment, he would see this man presenting to the buyers a young woman of a particular appearance. She would be wearing two layers of silk to shield herself from men's eyes and hands. “You will hear her cry aloud in Greek from beneath her delicate veil. Know that she will be saying: ‘Accursed be the man who uncovers my eyebrows!’” One of the men, moved by the young woman's modesty, would declare how greatly he wished to buy her.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01753

But she would answer: “Even if you possessed all the glory and riches of Solomon, son of David, I could never love you. Beware of wasting your wealth.” The shipowner, unwilling to force her, would admit his great embarrassment: the matter must somehow be settled. “Why such haste?” she would ask. “I must choose for myself the man who will buy me, so that my heart can find peace in the trust and fidelity I shall feel toward him.”
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01754

“At that moment, Bashar,” the Imam continued, “go up to Amr ibn Yazid and say: ‘I carry a letter, written in the Greek language and script (rumiya), by a noble man. It reveals his generosity, his loyalty, and his openhandedness. Give it to this young woman. Let her consider it and understand the character of its author. If she feels drawn to him and is satisfied, I am fully authorized to act on his behalf.’”
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01755

Everything happened exactly as the Imam had foretold, and Bashar followed his instructions. After reading the Imam's letter, the young woman let out an involuntary cry and told the shipowner that if he refused to sell her to the letter's author, she was prepared to take her own life.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01756

But events turned out as she wished. All Bashar had to do was bring her to his residence in Baghdad before setting off with her for Samarra. He noticed how happy and smiling she was, and how often she drew the letter from her bosom to press it to her lips, her eyes, and her eyebrows. Unable to restrain himself, he said: “Your behavior amazes me. You kiss a letter when you do not even know who wrote it!” She answered: “You poor man, so weak in faith! May knowledge of the spiritual rank of the Prophet's descendants dispel the doubts in your heart.”
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01757

Now we come to the marvelous story itself. From the outset, we should note that the young woman's ancestry is exactly what the recurring fullness of the Twelve requires. She continues: “Know that I am, in truth, a princess. My father is Yeshua, son of the emperor of Byzantium. My mother descends from the apostles of Christ. Her lineage goes back to Sham'un, Simon Peter, the wasi—the spiritual heir, or Imam—of the Lord Christ. I shall tell you my extraordinary story. My grandfather, the emperor, wished to marry me to his nephew.

passage-en-01758

“I was thirteen years old. He gathered an imposing assembly in his palace: three hundred clerics and monks, seven hundred members of the high nobility, and four thousand officers, military commanders, and landed nobles—five thousand people in all. Within the palace he had a throne erected at the top of forty steps, encrusted with jewels and precious stones of every kind. He seated his nephew on the throne, and around it was arranged a great assembly of icons (bot-ha, ‘idols’). The Christian priests stood before the throne with the deepest reverence. The Gospels were opened.

“But suddenly the idols came crashing down, the columns of the throne shattered, and my cousin fell with the throne to the floor and lost consciousness. Fear seized the dignitaries and notables; their faces changed with terror. Their leader declared: ‘O King, spare us the sight of these dreadful omens! Such an event foretells the decline and disappearance of the Christian religion.’ Deeply disturbed, my grandfather gave his orders: ‘Raise the columns of the throne again. Gather the icons back onto its summit. Bring my unfortunate nephew to me, so that I may celebrate his marriage to this girl and turn these sinister omens away from us.’

“But as the man who was the ornament of the assembly took his place for a second time, the same catastrophe occurred. This time the terrified gathering scattered in every direction. Troubled and saddened, my grandfather the emperor abandoned his plan and withdrew to his private rooms.”

After these striking omens comes a series of visionary dreams through which the young Byzantine princess receives her spiritual initiation.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01762

We can understand the first scene only if we remember the principle of correspondence that preserves the fullness of the Twelve from one era of prophecy to the next. Wherever this fullness appears, it carries the same secret of the same initiatory religion. What matters in the event as Shiite consciousness experiences it is that the passage from the Twelve of the Christian era to the Twelve of the Muhammadan era is completed and sealed through the mother of the Twelfth Muhammadan Imam. Through her, in the person of the young Byzantine princess, Christianity is initiated into Islam—or, more precisely, into Islamic gnosis, the inward knowledge of divine mysteries.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01763

And this mediation is born of a mystical, passionate love that first blossoms in a dream. The same principle of correspondence, so fundamental to Shiite thought, will be illustrated once again by the simultaneous presence of Fatima, mother of the holy Imams, and Mary, mother of Christ. In this visionary dream, Fatima takes on the role attributed to her by the more radical forms of Shiite gnosis, which name her Fatima-Fatir, Fatima the Creator—using the masculine form of “creator.” She is Initiation itself, embodied in a person.

passage-en-01764

“The night following these events,” the young woman tells Bashar, “I found myself in the world of visions. I saw the Lord Christ with his apostles inside the emperor's palace. At the very spot where the throne had stood the day before, they raised a pulpit (minbar) made entirely of light. Then Muhammad entered the palace with his wasi, his spiritual heir, and his glorious descendants—the holy Imams. Christ stepped forward to meet him and embraced the Prophet Muhammad. Muhammad said: ‘O Spirit of God (Ruh Allah), I have come to ask for the princess, the daughter of your wasi, Sham'un (Simon Peter), in marriage to my own son.’

“And he pointed toward Imam Hasan Askari. Christ looked long at Sham'un and said: ‘An extraordinary honor and nobility have come to you. Join your family, then, to the family of Muhammad.’ Sham'un replied: ‘It is done.’ Then all together—Muhammad and his Imams, Christ and his apostles—they climbed the steps to the top of the pulpit of light. There Muhammad delivered a magnificent sermon celebrating the marriage of his son and myself. Muhammad and his descendants, the holy Imams, and the apostles of Christ were all witnesses to our union.”

One cannot help imagining the grandeur of this scene unfolding in the church of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople.

The Shiite feeling expressed in this dream is the same one that inspired the great tenth-century Ismaili philosopher-theosopher Abu Ya'qub Sejestani to recognize the same meaning and structure in the Christian sign of the Cross and the Islamic declaration of the One God. Only those who penetrate to the hidden depths of religion seem capable of embracing this genuine fellowship across religious boundaries.

Remembering the conditions that have prevailed over the centuries of outward history, the student of religion may see in this dream an image as overwhelming as the vision experienced by Brother Marcus in the Goethe poem we shall quote later: the unfamiliar emblem of roses entwined around the Cross. The young Byzantine princess goes on: “When I awoke from this dream, I was afraid. I dared tell no one about it, for fear that my father and brother would kill me.

“I kept my secret so closely that my love for Imam Hasan Askari went on growing in my heart until I could no longer eat or drink. I grew thin, fell ill, and suffered terribly. There was not a physician in all the cities of the empire whom my father did not consult in the hope of curing me. One day, in despair, he said: ‘O light of my eyes! Is there any wish in your heart that I might fulfill?’ I answered: ‘The gates of joy are closed to me.

“But if you free the Muslim prisoners, perhaps Christ and his mother will come to my aid.’ When my father granted my wish, I showed some signs of returning health and began to eat again.

“Fourteen nights later, I had another dream. The sovereign of all womankind, Fatima the Radiant, came to visit me. Mary accompanied her, together with a thousand young women from among the houris of Paradise. Mary said to me: ‘Here is the Queen of Women, the mother of your husband, Imam Hasan Askari.’ I seized the hem of Fatima's robe and burst into tears. I complained that Imam Hasan had treated me so cruelly by refusing to let me see him.

“But Her Ladyship, Fatima, answered: ‘How could my child come to visit you while you continue to make God into many gods by remaining in the Christian religion? Here is my sister Mary. She has made herself free for God by leaving behind the religion you still profess.

“If you wish to please God, Mary, and Christ, and if you wish to see Imam Hasan Askari, then say: “I bear witness that there is no god but God, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God.”’ When I had spoken these two noble declarations, Fatima, Queen of Women, drew me to her and embraced me tightly. She said: ‘Now await my child's visit. I shall send him to you.’

“When I awoke, my tongue was still speaking those two noble declarations, and I waited to meet my Imam. When night came and I had returned to the world of visions, the sun of His Lordship's beauty rose before me. I said to him: ‘My beloved! Your love has made my heart its prisoner. Why have you withheld the sight of your beauty from me until now?’ He answered: ‘I was so long in coming to you because you were making God into many gods.

“Now that you have become a muslima, I shall be with you every night, until God brings us face to face, openly and without a veil, and replaces our separation with reunion.’ From that night until this very moment, not one night has passed without my beloved bringing me the drink of union to heal the pain of separation.”

Such is the secret entrusted to Bashar, the confidant of the holy Imams. He is familiar with the supernatural circumstances of life; those are not what he doubts. What troubles him is a thoroughly practical question. “How did you come to be among the captives?” he asks the young woman. She replies: “One night Imam Hasan Askari told me that my grandfather, the emperor, was about to send an army against the Muslims. He advised me to disguise myself so as not to be recognized, to take a few of my women with me, and to follow the army at a distance.
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01777

“I did as he said. Soon, as fortune would have it, a Muslim advance party came upon us and took us captive. That is how I came to be in the situation you now see. No one but you knows that I am the daughter of the emperor of Byzantium. When I was captured, an elder to whose share I had fallen asked me my name. Concealing my true name, I answered: ‘My name is Narcissus (Narkes).’”
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01778
Confronted with the wondrous story of a woman supernaturally called to become an Imam's companion, who had exposed herself to captivity out of pure love, Bashar can only remain respectfully silent.

Yet one last practical question concerns him, and he ventures to ask it: “You are Greek. How is it that you speak Arabic so well?” Narcissus explains: “My father took great care to give me an excellent education. He entrusted me to a woman highly skilled in several languages. She taught me Arabic morning and evening, until I became thoroughly proficient in it.”

Here ends what we might call the prologue to the mystery of the Twelfth Imam's birth. Now we enter the mystery itself. When Princess Narcissus (Narkes Khatun) is presented to Imam Ali Naqi at Samarra, the following dialogue takes place.

passage-en-01781

Imam Ali Naqi: In what way has God made known to you the glory of the Islamic religion and the error of the Christian religion, the exalted station of the Prophet and the members of his household—the holy Imams?
I. The Hagiography of the Twelfth Imam
passage-en-01782
Narcissus: How can I describe to you, O descendant of the Messenger of God, something you know so much better than I do?
